detail:
Oracle Stock Just Surged After CoreWeave Earnings. Here's Why One Analyst Says It's Built for the Data-Center Backlash
Jonathan Ponciano, The Motley Fool
Wed, November 11, 2026 at 3:11 PM MST 4 min read
ORCL
NVDA
CRWV

Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) shares rose nearly 9% to about $128 on Wednesday, part of a broad rally in AI stocks after AI cloud company CoreWeave (NASDAQ:CRWV) raised its revenue forecast and reported a massive order backlog of about $132.5 billion.

The jump follows a brutal stretch. Even after Wednesday's gain, Oracle is still down about 34% this year and more than 60% from its record levels last year.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.

Why CoreWeave's Results Mattered for Oracle

CoreWeave and Oracle are in the same business: renting out huge amounts of AI computing power. Both are spending heavily to build data centers, and investors have worried about how they'll pay for it.

CoreWeave's report eased some of that worry. Its CEO, Michael Intrator, said the company's growth is funded partly by "financing backed by customer contracts" and about $9 billion in customer prepayments and deposits expected in the next three months alone. In other words, customers are paying up front for capacity they want, which suggests demand for AI computing is real rather than speculative.

That obviously matters for Oracle, which is making the same kind of bet, but on a much bigger scale.

Why Oracle May Be Better Positioned

The latest worry for AI stocks is political. After last week's midterm elections, investors grew concerned that states and towns could restrict new data center construction. The restrictions have gotten bipartisan support. On Wednesday, Sen. Josh Hawley called for a moratorium on building them.

Still, analysts at Mizuho think Oracle is better prepared than most. In a note on Monday, the firm said all five of Oracle's mega sites are already under construction, and four have the necessary permits. The firm said potential delays are already built into Oracle's guidance, and that tighter permitting could even help Oracle by limiting new AI computing supply. Mizuho called the recent sell-off a buying opportunity and kept its Outperform rating.

The Demand Is There

Oracle's own numbers show why investors care. In its latest quarterly report, for the three months ended Aug. 31, cloud infrastructure revenue more than doubled to $7.4 billion. Total revenue rose 30% to $19.3 billion.

Its remaining performance obligations, or revenue it's already under contract to collect, reached $664 billion, up from $455 billion a year earlier. Oracle said the jump came mainly from "significant" (or, large) cloud contracts.

Artificial intelligence (AI) has become the biggest story, the central story, perhaps the only story that matters to the stock market right now. But many investors are getting anxious.

The past few months have been bad for AI stocks. The tech-heavy Nasdaq-100 officially entered a correction (a 10% or more decline), dropping 11.3% since Oct. 6 before gaining today. That's more than halfway to a bear market (a 20% or more decline).

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Some major tech names that have been driving the AI trade, such as Nvidia, CoreWeave, Tesla, Oracle, and Palantir, have seen significant share price declines over the past year.

NVDA data by YCharts

Does this mean that AI stocks are "over" and it's time to move your money to bonds or cash? Not necessarily. There are a few possible future paths for what might happen next with AI stocks and the broader stock market.

AI executives have made some incredibly lofty predictions about what their technology might do in the future. We've heard bold claims that AI will boost U.S. GDP by 50% in just four years, but also that it will replace most entry-level white-collar jobs, or even be responsible for the extinction of mankind. I'm skeptical about these most extreme scenarios.

At the other extreme, some AI skeptics believe the technology is overrated, overpriced, and unlikely to deliver meaningful gains in productivity or economic growth. I feel like this is unlikely to be true for too long. Companies across industries are experimenting with AI to improve their processes, save time, and reduce costs. Are we really supposed to believe that all that effort will amount to nothing, that AI is just going to "go away"? I doubt that.

Instead, I think it's more likely that we find a happier middle ground on the future of AI.

Let's take a big-picture look at the future of AI stocks -- with optimistic (bull case), pessimistic (bear case), and middle-ground (base case) scenarios. And let's see how you could position your investments based on which outcome you think is most likely.

Image source: Getty Images.
Bull case: Today's AI stock winners keep winning

AI doesn't destroy human civilization or take all the jobs. Instead, it delivers game-changing productivity growth. Good news comes out about a highly popular, profitable new AI product that's a game changer, like Google search was in 1999 or the iPhone in 2007. Or AI gets cheaper to build. (Or both.)

Key Takeaways

Oracle CFO Hilary Maxson told CNBC that Oracle will be cash-flow positive in the second half of fiscal 2028 and produce more than $30 billion of free cash flow in fiscal 2029, days after Oracle lost a Tencent deal.

Her case rests on capital spending peaking. Oracle says its recent $20 billion raise is all the outside money it needs, so spending has to stop climbing while its $664 billion backlog starts paying.

Analysts expect $17.5 billion of free cash flow in fiscal 2029, well below the target, and total debt reached $169.1 billion by Aug. 31.

The cap on new funding makes the turn more believable than the stock's fall suggests, and OpenAI's ability to pay is the main risk.

Oracle (ORCL:NYSE) had a brutal week before its CFO ever went on air. In three days, it lost a roughly $7 billion Tencent deal and a contract with Microsoft (MSFT).

On Nov. 10, Hilary Maxson sat down with David Faber on CNBC's Squawk on the Street. It was her first broadcast interview as Oracle's CFO, and she put dates on the recovery.

"We're fully funded, cash flow positive in the second half of our 28, $30 billion plus free cash flow in 29," she said.

That's quite a promise from a company that burned $23.7 billion of free cash flow in fiscal 2026, the year ended May 2026.

title: ServiceNow Drops 29% in a Month: Should You Hold or Fold the Stock?
detail:
ServiceNow Drops 29% in a Month: Should You Hold or Fold the Stock?

ORCL

CRM
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

ServiceNow NOW shares have dropped 29% in the past month, underperforming the broader Zacks Computer and Technology sector's fall of 12.6%. The company's shares have also lagged peers, including Oracle ORCL, Salesforce CRM and Microsoft MSFT, shares of which have declined 14.1%, 8.7% and 28.5%, respectively, over the same time frame. NOW's underperformance can be attributed to investor concerns over slowing near-term backlog growth, modest guidance increases, acquisition-related risks and uncertainty over the monetization of artificial intelligence (AI). Let's delve deep to find out what investors should do with the NOW stock.

NOW Stock's Price Performance
Zacks Investment Research

Image Source: Zacks Investment Research

NOW Stock Suffers From Modest Expectations

ServiceNow's fourth-quarter 2026 current remaining performance obligations (cRPO) outlook has been disappointing. The company expects cRPO growth of 18.5% in constant currency (cc) compared with 21% in the third quarter of 2026. The projected slowdown has raised concerns about future subscription revenue growth. NOW attributed the deceleration to early renewals in the third quarter, a higher mix of on-premises public-sector contracts, deployment-related accounting adjustments and termination-for-convenience provisions that exclude certain backlog from cRPO.

ServiceNow raised its 2026 subscription revenue guidance by only $15 million at the midpoint, to $15.785 billion. This relatively small increase may have disappointed investors expecting a stronger outlook from the company's accelerating AI business. NOW explained that its decision to include deployment expertise with certain large customer agreements is shifting some revenues from subscriptions to professional services. This reduced subscription revenue growth by approximately 25 basis points (bps) in the third quarter and is expected to create a 50-bps headwind in the fourth quarter.

ServiceNow's expansion through acquisitions is another potential source of investor concern. The company's Armis acquisition is expected to contribute approximately 175 bps to fourth-quarter subscription revenue growth in cc but reduce non-GAAP operating margin by approximately 75 bps. NOW's growing exposure to cybersecurity also increases integration complexity as it combines acquired technologies with its broader AI platform.

NOW Faces Profitability and Debt Challenges

ServiceNow faces mounting profitability challenges due to higher infrastructure expenses and acquisition-related costs. In the third quarter of 2026, subscription cost of revenues increased 58% year over year to $1.05 billion, significantly outpacing subscription revenue growth of 21%. Consequently, GAAP subscription gross margin contracted to approximately 74% from 80% in the year-ago quarter. Higher third-party cloud expenses, employee costs and amortization of acquired intangible assets contributed to the deterioration. Sustained investment in AI infrastructure and cybersecurity offerings could continue to pressure profitability despite improving operating efficiencies.

The Zacks Consensus Estimate for NOW's 2026 earnings has declined by 2.7% to $3.95 per share over the past 30 days and indicates 12.5% growth from 2025's reported figure. The consensus mark for NOW's fourth-quarter 2026 earnings estimate is currently pegged at $1.08 per share, down 6.1% over the past 30 days and suggests 17.4% growth over the figure reported in the year-ago quarter.

Key Takeaways

Oracle stock is down 50% from its June high. On Nov. 10, Bernstein kept its Outperform rating and $325 target, which is 159% above the price.

Bernstein sees Oracle's data center and database businesses as long-term AI winners and names two catalysts: an OpenAI IPO and positive free cash flow in the second half of fiscal 2028.

Analysts have raised their earnings estimates even as the stock fell, so Oracle trades at about 14x forward earnings against a five-year average of 21x.

The selloff looks overdone. But $325 needs about 38x forward earnings while Oracle is still raising money, and that's too much to expect within a year.

Oracle (ORCL:NYSE) stock is down 50% from its June high, and Bernstein still isn't budging. On Nov. 10, analyst Mark Moerdler kept his Outperform rating and $325 price target, 159% above where the stock trades now.

The bills came first, then the bad news

The slide started with the cost of Oracle's AI build. S&P cut Oracle's credit rating to BBB- in July. In the quarter to Aug. 31, capex hit $28.5 billion, free cash flow was negative $5 billion, and Oracle finished a $20 billion stock sale. On Nov. 2, it priced another $20 billion raise in new shares and notes.

Then November piled on. Oracle canceled a chip-leasing deal with Tencent worth an estimated $7 billion, the Financial Times reported. AI build-out stocks sold off on Nov. 5 after Democrats won both chambers of Congress. And on Nov. 6, Bloomberg reported that Microsoft is winding down a deal to rent AI computing from Oracle.
